title: 2026 ACC Chief Legal Officers Survey
pub: Association of Corporate Counsel, presented by FTI Consulting
author: Association of Corporate Counsel

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The survey accepts the cluster’s core account of workflow reconfiguration rather than wholesale lawyer replacement and materially extends it with buyer-side evidence: most CLOs expect stable headcount alongside substantial role evolution, with planning centred on skills and process redesign. It provides adoption and workforce expectations, however, rather than evidence about realised productivity, verification burdens or competence risks.
qs: The overwhelming majority, 63%, anticipate that legal department headcount will stay similar, but that existing roles will evolve significantly due to AI integration.
These figures suggest that, over the next three to five years, strategic planning will be focused heavily on skill transformation and process refinement, not aggressive hiring or deep staff cuts.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: ACC accepts the work-redesign proposition and adds buyer-side survey evidence: most CLOs expect AI to transform roles and processes rather than materially reduce headcount, while value depends on skills, operational foundations and resource investment. Its contribution is directional and forward-looking, based on self-reported expectations rather than measured productivity or employment effects.
qs: The overwhelming majority, 63%, anticipate that legal department headcount will stay similar, but that existing roles will evolve significantly due to AI integration.

For the modern legal department, technology is increasingly viewed as            the essential bridge between rising workloads and stagnant budgets—a tool not for reducing            headcount, but for unlocking the “resource elasticity” required to support rapid business changes.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s bounded view: substantial deployment and shifting investment priorities show organisational adoption, but they do not establish investment value. Its explanations for declining mature-tool priorities are explicitly possibilities—successful prior adoption or anticipated AI integration/supersession—not demonstrated causes or ROI evidence.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s core view that legal departments are prioritising AI-enabled operational change under resource constraints, with organisational capabilities and role redesign more salient than immediate headcount reduction. Its rising reliance on outside providers tempers any strong near-term insourcing claim but is consistent with the cluster’s caution that buyer transformation remains incomplete.
qs: The success of            the department hinges on leveraging AI to solve the financial and            efficiency problems that currently impede adoption.
The overwhelming majority, 63%, anticipate that legal department headcount will stay similar, but that existing roles will evolve significantly due to AI integration.

st.t: Legal departments: AI supports selective sourcing redesign
st.an: The ACC survey directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: constrained resources are driving AI-enabled operating-model changes focused on efficiency, role evolution and flexible capacity rather than headcount reduction. It also supports selective sourcing redesign through a hybrid model that keeps internal staffing stable while increasing reliance on outside counsel and consultants. Its claims about competitive advantage remain forward-looking prescriptions rather than demonstrated business value, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: To bridge this gap, CLOs have identified operational efficiency (53%) as their top strategic initiative for 2026, leveraging AI not to reduce headcount, but to evolve roles and automate routine tasks.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s rejection of wholesale lawyer replacement by framing GenAI as augmenting existing in-house talent and redirecting work toward higher-value strategic activity. Its evidence is limited to current deployment and CLO expectations, so it does not establish actual staffing effects or materially develop the cluster’s implementation, verification or evaluation framework.
qs: However, this is not viewed      as a replacement for human talent; 63% of CLOs expect headcount to      remain stable, focusing instead on evolving existing roles to focus on      higher-value strategic work through AI-driven efficiency.

kp.k: Survey captures buyer-side expectations from late 2025
kp.d: The ACC survey, conducted in collaboration with FTI Consulting, reports responses from 1,049 CLOs and highest-ranked legal officers across 43 countries, collected September 10–November 7, 2025. The participant profile is 64% United States. These are reported experiences and expectations, with question-specific response bases, rather than observed future outcomes.
qs: Data collection occurred over an eight-week fielding period, from September 10 to November 7, 2025.
Not all respondents for every question.

kp.k: CLO executive status strengthens while functional expansion stabilizes
kp.d: The survey reports 84% directly reporting to the CEO, 79% almost always attending board meetings, and adoption of the CLO title increasing from 25% in 2025 to 34% in 2026. General Counsel remains the most common title. Meanwhile, oversight of two or more functions beyond legal or compliance settled around 69%, below the 77% peak in 2023; the report interprets this as stabilization and specialization rather than continuing expansion.
qs: The share of CLOs leaped from 25% in 2025 to a high of 34% in 2026.

The role appears to be entering a period of specialization, intensely focusing on its core governance and risk competencies while largely avoiding further expansion into operational areas like finance, marketing, or IT.

kp.k: Strategic influence grows, with important subgroup qualifications
kp.d: Across respondents, 47% report deeper and more frequent board-level and C-suite strategic engagement over the preceding three years, while 37% report expanded scope. Among that latter subgroup, 74% report increased proactive strategic counsel, 65% increased enterprise-wide risk input, and 42% increased input into innovation, technology and AI strategy. The 74% finding is therefore not a measure of all surveyed CLOs contributing to corporate strategy.
qs: Among the 37% of CLOs who reported an expansion in the scope and areas of their board involvement over the past three years, respondents were asked to identify the specific strategic areas where their input has become more significant.
The top area, with 74% of respondents, is the growth in providing proactive strategic counsel, confirming that legal guidance is now integral to long-term planning.

kp.k: AI proficiency leads perceived CEO development priorities
kp.d: Technology and AI knowledge and strategy is selected by 47% as an area respondents believe their CEO wants them to develop, ahead of business acumen at 34%. This measures CLO perceptions, not direct CEO responses. Technology/AI and operational efficiency were newly offered options, limiting longitudinal comparisons. AI proficiency and business integration each receive 15% as the single most significant skill developed over the preceding three years.
qs: In which areas do you believe the CEO would like you to further develop? Select all that apply.
The response options “Technology and AI knowledge/strategy” and “Operational efficiency” were not offered in previous years.

kp.k: Lawyer development emphasizes business and technological capabilities
kp.d: Business acumen leads departmental lawyer development priorities at 68%, followed by communication at 45% and executive presence at 43%. Technological fluency rises from 17% in 2024 to 22% in 2025 and 34% in 2026. The detailed table thus places the 17-point increase over two years, although an earlier key finding describes it as occurring in a single year.
qs: Which of the following skills are you seeking to develop for the lawyers in your department? Select all that apply.
Business acumen (68%) is the top skill development priority for departmental lawyers.

kp.k: New technology plans prioritize generative AI
kp.d: The share planning new legal technology within 12 months reaches 52%, compared with 42% in 2021. Among those planning new solutions, 69% identify generative AI for increased investment over the next 24 months, ahead of contract management at 55%. Generative AI was a newly offered response option, so its ranking does not establish a measured year-on-year increase.
qs: The percentage of CLOs planning on adopting new solutions has steadily increased over the past six years, rising from 42% in 2021 to a high of 52% in 2026.
The response options “Generative AI”, “Legal research tools”, and “Corporate secretary management” were not offered in previous years.

kp.k: Foundational tool priorities decline alongside AI investment
kp.d: The report identifies declining investment prioritization for collaboration and knowledge management, workflow, document management and matter management tools. Contract management falls nine points from 2024 to 55%. It suggests successful prior adoption or anticipated integration and substitution by newer technologies as possible explanations, rather than establishing that AI has already replaced these systems.
qs: Investment is Shifting Away from Foundational Tools
departments have successfully adopted these tools already, or newer, more powerful technologies are expected to integrate or supersede the functions of these older tools.

kp.k: AI adoption spans testing, implementation and reported results
kp.d: The adoption breakdown is 36% cautiously testing, 22% implemented for selected tasks, 14% embracing AI with results already seen, and 9% working toward broad implementation. The report groups the latter three as 45% beyond testing, although this includes implementation in progress; its earlier 36% active-deployment headline corresponds to the two implemented/results categories. Non-adoption is attributed to risk concerns by 6%, cost by 4%, and other reasons by 6%.
qs: WE ARE TESTING POTENTIAL USE CASES CAUTIOUSLY
WE HAVE IMPLEMENTED IT FOR SELECT TASKS OR USE CASES
WE ARE EMBRACING GENERATIVE AI AND HAVE ALREADY SEEN RESULTS
WE ARE WORKING TO IMPLEMENT IT BROADLY FOR NUMEROUS TASKS AND USE CASES

kp.k: Expected AI impact favors role evolution over cuts
kp.d: Looking three to five years ahead, 63% expect similar legal department headcount with evolving roles, 9% expect net reductions, 4% increases from new needs, and 23% remain uncertain. The report interprets this as an augmentation and routine-task automation orientation. These are staffing predictions, not evidence that AI has already preserved jobs or improved productivity.
qs: A notable 23% remain uncertain or feel it is too early to tell what the true staffing impact will be.
Only a small fraction of CLOs anticipates extreme outcomes: 9% predict a net reduction in headcount, while 4% foresee a net increase due to the creation of new AI-related needs.

kp.k: Near-term staffing expectations remain predominantly stable
kp.d: For the next 12 months, 56% expect lawyer staffing to stay unchanged, 33% an increase and 6% a decrease. Expectations of increases are 22% for paralegals, 13% for legal operations professionals, 16% for other allied professionals and 9% for administrative staff. These general staffing plans are distinct from the longer-term AI-specific staffing question.
qs: Do you anticipate your department’s staffing levels will decrease, stay the same, or increase in the next 12 months?

This points to a strategy of reinforcing high-value, specialized functions (lawyers and legal operations) with limited expansion, while finding ways to maintain or slightly reduce administrative support.

kp.d: In a multiple-response question, 33% report distributing legal operations responsibilities across team members, 18% a dedicated tactical professional, 7% strategic advisory professionals and 9% professionals empowered to manage programs and make departmental business decisions. Only 10% measure benefits and 20% want additional investment. The report suggests small department scale may partly explain limited formalization; its grouped maturity totals should not be treated as mutually exclusive population shares.
qs: How is your department leveraging the legal operations function? Select all that apply.
This is likely heavily driven by a significant portion of CLO respondents who lead small law departments and are therefore not at sufficient scale to set up a distinct legal ops function.

kp.k: Law firm growth expectations moderate; ALSP expectations stabilize
kp.d: The proportion expecting to increase work sent to law firms falls from 43% in 2025 to 37% in 2026; 45% expect no change and 18% a decrease. For other legal service providers, 18% expect an increase, 72% no change and 10% a decrease. The report interprets ALSPs as a steadier component of resourcing, not as demonstrating an AI-driven transfer of work away from firms.
qs: Anticipation for increasing work sent to law firms decreased noticeably from 43% in 2025 to 37% in 2026.

This indicates that ALSPs may be viewed as a constant, non-cyclical part of the resourcing mix, whereas traditional law firms are utilized more dynamically based on immediate market and operational needs.

kp.k: Regulatory pressure increases reliance on external expertise
kp.d: Looking retrospectively at responses to global regulatory risk, 48% report increased reliance on outside counsel, versus 43% previously, and 27% increased consultant reliance, versus 21%. Internal hiring generally remains unchanged. These figures measure increased reliance, not the overall proportion using counsel or consultants, and differ from the forward-looking outsourcing question. Meanwhile, 59% report rising litigation costs and 42% rising litigation volume.
qs: reliance on outside counsel jumped from 43% to 48%, and reliance on consultants saw a six-point rise from 21% to 27%.
Critically, the cost of litigation remains the most significant area of reported increase, cited by 59% in 2026, only slightly down from 60% in 2025.

kp.k: AI regulation becomes a growing enforcement concern
kp.d: Among respondents selecting their top three enforcement concerns, AI regulation rises from 19% in 2025 to 24% in 2026. Trade/tariffs receives 30% but is newly offered, so no comparable growth rate is available. Industry-specific regulation remains highest at 64%. Separately, 11% observe regulators using advanced analytics or AI, and 8% increased enforcement in emerging technology spaces.
qs: Similarly, concern over AI regulation saw the largest percentage point increase, climbing five points to 24%, confirming it as a clear emerging priority.
The response option “Trade/tariffs” was not offered the previous year.

kp.k: Political risk changes counsel selection for a minority
kp.d: Thirteen percent globally report changing outside counsel evaluation and selection in response to US political developments. Among that subgroup, 41% added political or reputational risk categories, 37% ceased working with particular firms, and 26% began formalizing third-party risk management. These conditional findings concern external provider selection, not demonstrated consequences of AI.
qs: While the majority of organizations (87%) have maintained their existing approach, a noteworthy minority (13% of all global participants) report that they have changed their evaluation and selection criteria due to recent political developments in the United States.
Only asked to those who said they have changed their approach to evaluating and selecting outside counsel.

kp.k: Resource constraints complicate AI-led operational transformation
kp.d: AI and technology adoption is identified as the most frequently mentioned urgent issue in open-ended responses, without a numerical share. Budget and resources are the greatest barrier for 35%, and talent and staffing for 19%. Operational efficiency leads next-12-month strategic initiatives at 53%, followed by regulatory compliance at 39% and technology implementation at 38%. The report recommends using AI to address efficiency constraints; that is a proposed response rather than a demonstrated solution.
qs: Budget and resources are cited as the single greatest barrier by a commanding 35% of respondents, making it the most critical constraint on departmental effectiveness.
Operational efficiency is the number one strategic initiative (53%), closely followed by regulatory compliance (39%) and technology implementation (38%).
Success hinges on leveraging AI as the solution to the efficiency problem, rather than allowing it to become another unchecked regulatory risk.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: ACC presents generative AI as a driver of in-house legal role transformation, technology investment, leadership development and regulatory work, primarily through augmentation rather than headcount reduction.
pts.d: The ACC report, presented by FTI Consulting, makes six connected claims. First, AI is expected to automate routine tasks and change existing legal roles rather than principally replace employees: 63% of CLOs expect similar headcount with evolving roles, compared with 9% expecting reductions, 4% increases and 23% uncertainty. Second, adoption is moving beyond exploration: 36% are cautiously testing, 22% have implemented selected uses, 14% have embraced GenAI and seen results, and 9% are working toward broad implementation. The report groups the latter three categories as 45% moving beyond testing; its earlier key findings use 36% for active deployment. Third, GenAI is the leading planned technology investment, selected by 69% of CLOs planning new solutions. ACC suggests that declining prioritization of foundational tools may reflect previous adoption or expectations that GenAI will integrate or supersede their functions; this is an interpretation rather than a demonstrated substitution outcome. Fourth, AI creates new leadership and lawyer-development priorities, combining technological fluency with business strategy. Fifth, the report frames AI as a potential means of addressing constrained resources and rising workloads, while those same constraints impede transformation. Sixth, AI adds regulatory concerns and appears in regulators’ own tools: 24% identify AI regulation among their top three enforcement concerns, and 11% report regulators’ use of advanced analytics/AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of CLO survey responses and qualitative comments, not measured AI performance or independently verified staffing and productivity effects.
pts.d: ACC surveyed 1,049 CLOs and highest-ranked legal officers across 43 countries using an online questionnaire, with outreach through ACC members, partner organizations and LinkedIn. Responses provide self-reported adoption, priorities, perceived executive expectations and staffing forecasts. The sample is 64% US-based and includes departments of different sizes; 55% report fewer than ten legal staff. Question bases vary with valid responses, multiple-response questions can exceed 100%, and rounding can affect totals. The claim that AI and technology adoption is the most urgent issue comes from thematic grouping of open-ended comments, without a numerical share reported for that theme. Quantitative skill evidence includes 47% identifying technology and AI knowledge/strategy as an area they believe their CEO wants developed, 15% naming AI and technology proficiency as their single most significant recently developed competency, and 34% prioritizing technological fluency for departmental lawyers. The detailed chart gives technological fluency as 17% in 2024, 22% in 2025 and 34% in 2026: the 17-point increase spans 2024–2026, although the key findings describe it as occurring in a single year. GenAI investment and technology/AI development expectations were new response options, so those categories do not supply direct year-over-year comparisons. The report offers no quantified task-time savings, output-quality benchmarks or causal estimate of AI-driven employment change. Its explanation that GenAI may supersede foundational tools and its resource-elasticity argument are interpretive claims based on the survey patterns.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 report records late-2025 responses, with separate horizons for adoption, investment, skill development and expected staffing effects.
pts.d: Fieldwork ran from September 10 to November 7, 2025. Current GenAI adoption figures describe respondents’ positions during that period, not independently observed deployments later in 2026. New legal technology adoption plans concern the next 12 months; 52% plan adoption. Technology investment priorities concern the next 24 months, framed by the report as 2026–2027, with the 69% GenAI figure attributed to CLOs planning new solutions. AI staffing expectations cover the next three to five years and remain forecasts, including substantial uncertainty. Personal competency development and expanded strategic board input refer retrospectively to the preceding three years. The report’s suggestion that GenAI will integrate or supersede existing tools is conditional on departments’ prior adoption or expectations of new technologies. Non-adoption is attributed to risk/concerns by 6%, cost by 4% and other reasons by 6%. The operational transformation argument is conditioned by resource scarcity: 35% identify budget/resources as their greatest barrier, while operational efficiency and technology implementation are selected as next-12-month strategic initiatives by 53% and 38%, respectively.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected population is the corporate buyer side: CLOs, in-house lawyers and their legal departments, with implications for enterprise governance and technology purchasing.
pts.d: For CLOs, ACC describes an expanding expectation of technological knowledge, AI strategy and business leadership. Among the 37% reporting expanded scope in board involvement over the preceding three years, 42% report more significant input into innovation, technology and AI strategy; that percentage is not a share of all surveyed CLOs. For departmental lawyers, the predicted effect is changed tasks and greater demand for technological fluency and business acumen, rather than majority expectations of job cuts. For legal departments and their internal business clients, AI is presented as a way to improve efficiency and maintain support for business growth despite resource constraints. For the legal-technology market, planned spending priorities favor GenAI over some foundational categories, without establishing actual vendor revenue shifts. For corporate compliance teams, AI brings regulatory concerns and exposure to regulators using analytics or AI. The report separately records law-firm and ALSP resourcing expectations, but does not establish that AI caused those patterns or predict AI-driven displacement of either provider group. It does not offer specific findings on access to justice, public-facing legal assistance, junior-lawyer displacement or law-firm staffing structures.
